title: 🔥 Streaming Write + Concurrent Search, Without the P99 Spike
content: Agent workloads are continuous write + millisecond-later read. seekdb's async index pipeline (Change Stream) decouples DML from index build, and its two-level HNSW (incremental + snapshot) makes newly-written vectors immediately searchable. The write path commits and returns without waiting on index construction.

title: 🔥 Streaming Write + Concurrent Search, Without the P99 Spike
content: Queries hit both delta and snapshot indexes with fine-grained read locks — this is why P99 stays flat under concurrency. The result: 1,523 QPS with 21.7 ms concurrent P99 — 10.7× the QPS of Milvus, and P99 jitter of just 1.1× when concurrency rises (vs ~10× for ES / Milvus on the same workload). Source: src/observer/change stream/ · src/observer/vector index/

title: You're Using the Wrong Benchmark to Choose a Vector Database for Your Agent
content: The real workload of an Agent is a streaming workload — most vector databases weren't designed for it. If you're choosing a vector database for your Agent, you're probably looking at ann-benchmarks or the performance comparisons published by each vendor. Those tests run a workload like this: bulk-import all the data, build the index, then run read-only queries.

title: You're Using the Wrong Benchmark to Choose a Vector Database for Your Agent
content: VectorDBBench designed its StreamingPerformanceCase specifically for this: continuous writes at a fixed rate + concurrent queries, exactly like a production Agent. VectorDBBench is maintained by Zilliz (the company behind Milvus) and is a third-party open-source benchmark framework. We used it to test 6 mainstream vector databases.

title: A Metric Everyone Ignores: How Much Does Your P99 Spike Under Concurrency?
content: What actually determines your SLA is the concurrent P99 — and how much it spikes as concurrency increases. Look at the "P99 Jitter" group in the chart: - ES: 10.3x — serial P99 is only 5.2ms (faster than seekdb), but once concurrency kicks in it jumps to 53.6ms - Milvus: 9.7x — serial 15.9ms, concurrent spikes straight to 153.6ms - seekdb: 1.1x — from 19.7ms to 21.7ms, barely moves This isn't a parameter-tuning issue — it's an architecture issue.

title: Why P99 Explodes Under Streaming Workloads
content: This is barely manageable single-threaded, but once concurrency ramps up, N segments x M query threads contend for CPU, and P99 skyrockets. Most vector databases see their segment count balloon with streaming writes, making concurrent query contention progressively worse.

title: Why P99 Explodes Under Streaming Workloads
content: Writes and index building are physically decoupled — writes are never blocked by index construction. Second, the query path always hits exactly two indexes. seekdb maintains a delta HNSW (incremental layer, receives new writes) and a snapshot HNSW (main base layer), similar to the tiered approach of an LSM-Tree.

title: Why P99 Explodes Under Streaming Workloads
content: After the rewrite, same product, 22x QPS improvement, P99 latency reduced by 19x — all from these two mechanisms.

title: Agents Need More Than Speed — They Need an Undo Button
content: seekdb implements Copy-on-Write directly in the kernel: This is kernel-level COW, not application-layer snapshot/restore.

title: Hybrid Retrieval in a Single SQL Statement
content: In seekdb, that's a single SQL statement: Vector + full-text + scalar filtering are pushed down within the same execution plan — no need to assemble multiple query results on the client side.

title: About seekdb
content: seekdb is fully open source (Apache 2.0), developed by the OceanBase team. You may already be using OceanBase — it runs in production at Alipay, Taobao, DiDi, Xiaomi, and more. seekdb inherits the same storage engine and SQL executor, focused on the vector + relational hybrid workload for Agent scenarios — with 2,500+ GitHub stars since launch and integrations with LangChain / LlamaIndex / Dify / Coze and other major frameworks.

title: その Benchmark で Agent のベクトルデータベースを選ぶのは間違いだ
content: Agent の実際の負荷は streaming workload です——ほとんどのベクトルデータベースはそのために設計されていません。 もしあなたが Agent 用のベクトルデータベースを選んでいるなら、おそらく ann-benchmarks や各社が公式に出している性能比較を参考にしているでしょう。それらのテストが実行しているのはこのような負荷です：まずデータを一括インポートし、インデックスを構築してから、読み取り専用のクエリを実行する。

title: 見落とされている指標：並行処理時に P99 はどれだけ悪化するのか？
content: テスト条件：Cohere 10M データセット（768 次元）、16 vCPU / 64 GiB、統一 HNSW インデックスパラメータ（M=16 / ef construction=256 / ef search=200）、継続的に 500 行/秒で書き込み。

title: なぜ streaming 負荷で P99 が爆発するのか
content: Milvus、ES、Qdrant はそれぞれが得意とするシナリオ（一括インポート + 読み取り専用クエリ）では優れたパフォーマンスを発揮します——もともとそのシナリオのために設計されているからです。しかし streaming 書き込みは構造的な問題を露呈させます：新しい segment が次々と生成されるのです。クエリ時には N 個の segment それぞれに対して fanout して knn を実行し、結果をマージする必要があります。シングルスレッドであればなんとか制御可能ですが、 並行度が上がると、N 個の segment × M 個のクエリスレッドが CPU 上で互いに競合し、P99 が急上昇します。 ほとんどのベクトルデータベースでは、streaming 書き込みに伴いインデックスの segment 数が膨張し、並行クエリの競合が悪化し続けます。seekdb のインデックス数は固定です（常に 2 つだけ）ので、この問題は発生しません。 具体的には、seekdb v1.3.0 は streaming 負荷のために 2 つのメカニズムを設計しました： 第一に、書き込みパスはインデックスに触れません。 トランザクションのコミット後は redo log を書くだけで即座に返します。独立した Change Stream パイプラインがバックグラウンドで非同期に redo log を消費し、ベクトルをメモリ上の delta HNSW インデックスに書き込みます。書き込みとインデックス構築は物理的に完全に分離されており——書き込みがインデックス構築によってブロックされることはありません。

title: Agent に必要なのは速さだけではない——「やり直し」の仕組みも必要
content: パフォーマンスについては説明しました。しかし Agent を開発したことがある方なら、もう一つの課題をご存知でしょう：Agent は試行錯誤的にデータを変更する必要があります（memory の書き換え、実験の実行、テーブルの破壊的変更など）。 安全なサンドボックスとロールバックの仕組みが必要です。 ほとんどのベクトルデータベースにはこの概念がありません。seekdb はカーネルレベルで Copy-on-Write を実装しています： これはカーネルレベルの COW であり、アプリケーション層の snapshot/restore ではありません。fork は秒単位で完了し、データのコピーは行わず、各サンドボックスは完全に書き込み可能なデータベースです（テーブル構造、ベクトルインデックス、自動インクリメントカラムすべてが正常に動作します）。3 つのコンフリクト戦略（ FAIL / THEIRS / OURS ）により、Agent の変更をどこまで信頼するかを精密に制御できます。 FORK DATABASE と FORK TABLE の 2 つの粒度をサポートしています。

title: Set build concurrency
content: Bazel defaults to the available host CPU count. When you explicitly set local build concurrency, build.py sets both the job limit and the local CPU scheduling budget: -j32 , -j 32 , and --jobs=32 are equivalent. Only explicit numeric command-line values are synchronized; omitting the option preserves Bazel's automatic defaults. An explicit --local resources=cpu=N overrides this budget. Memory settings are unaffected.

title: Use remote C++ compilation
content: Specify your REAPI service address and concurrency: The default strategies in .bazelrc prefer remote execution for C++ compilation and use local execution when no remote executor is configured. Set --remote executor without adding --config=remote . Rust compilation, generators, and linking run locally.

title: Use remote C++ compilation
content: Bazel still detects the local CPU budget automatically unless you set it separately with --local resources=cpu=N .

title: Build directories
content: For example, ./build.py build -o build3 seekdb uses build3/ as the working directory and build3/bin/src/observer/seekdb as the binary path. Relative paths are resolved from the project root; absolute paths can place builds on another disk. Different directories have independent build state and links and can build concurrently. Bazel serializes commands using the same directory.

title: Reuse build caches
content: Bazel binaries and the default action cache are shared between checkouts. Their base directory is ~/.cache/bazel on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/bazel on macOS, or %LOCALAPPDATA%/bazel on Windows. Linux honors XDG CACHE HOME . Bazel manages its shared repository download cache separately. Use --launcher cache dir PATH for the Bazel binary cache, --disk cache=PATH for build actions, or --repository cache=PATH for downloaded dependencies. All go after the command.

title: 1. Keep dependencies directed from C++ to Rust by default
content: Keep Rust core modules independent and concentrate cross-language adaptation at their boundaries. Prefer explicit inputs, returned results, and orchestration by callers to connect the two languages. Use cross-language callbacks or interface injection when needed. Do not add queues, event protocols, or extra threads solely to avoid callbacks.

title: 2. Design native interfaces for Rust callers and use CXX for compatibility
content: Design natural Rust types, ownership, and error models first. Then adapt existing C++ types, error codes, and calling conventions. CXX representation constraints should not determine the core interface. Rust callers must be able to use the full capability through native interfaces without constructing bridge objects or following C++ compatibility conventions. Use the repository's existing CXX bridges and build integration for interoperability in both directions.

title: 3. Pass business state explicitly and allow appropriate infrastructure access
content: Give context that affects business correctness an explicit owner and pass it through parameters or handles. Each module receives only the state and capabilities it needs. Avoid hiding dependencies in an all-purpose context object. A global entry point can be appropriate for cross-cutting infrastructure with process-wide semantics that needs no isolation per request or instance, such as a logger.

title: 5. Migrate complete responsibilities and preserve module cohesion
content: Check whether adjacent state management, validation, resource management, error handling, and platform adaptation should move into Rust together. Avoid moving only low-level functions while leaving most complexity in C++. Choose scope by responsibility and dependencies rather than migrated line count. Organize modules around state ownership, invariants, and reasons to change together. Do not mechanically reproduce C++ classes, files, or inheritance hierarchies.

title: 6. Redesign around behavior contracts
content: Before choosing data structures or execution mechanisms, identify the behavior callers need and the invariants the implementation must preserve. Redesign internals when useful rather than translating line by line. For each task, define compatibility requirements for external behavior, data formats, durability, and recovery.

title: 7. Express valid states through types and ownership
content: Use domain types, enums, and handles with explicit lifetimes to express important states. Reduce invalid combinations and implicit call ordering. Parse and validate external input at boundaries. Use types that carry established constraints in internal interfaces. Keep resources alive until their actual users finish. Logical completion, cancellation, or timeout does not imply that background work has stopped.

title: 8. Define concurrency protocols before choosing synchronization mechanisms
content: Define who can mutate state, when an operation is accepted, how results are published, and how cancellation and shutdown finish. Reduce shared mutable state before choosing locks, atomics, or message passing. Different modules may use different concurrency models. When introducing queues or background work, define capacity, backpressure, and resource limits.

title: 9. Switch production callers and remove replaced implementations
content: Maintain necessary long-term interfaces through clear contracts. An adapter or callback does not by itself make a design temporary.

title: 10. Validate behavior according to risk
content: Distinguish unsupported capabilities from actual failures. Compilation alone does not prove that a migration is complete. For performance-sensitive paths, compare the baseline and new implementation with equivalent semantics and workloads. Report the results, environment, and coverage gaps. Do not hide regressions by reducing functionality.

title: Task deliverables
content: When departing from a default principle, explain the specific constraint, impact, and scope. Do not turn an exception into the default for unrelated modules.

title: seekdb WebAssembly shell
content: A browser SQL shell backed by the seekdb engine compiled to WebAssembly. The terminal layout, command history, and example entry point take inspiration from the Lite4MariaDB shell. Its JavaScript SDK and Worker API also informed the loading, result, error, and close behavior. This shell uses seekdb's existing JavaScript API and WebAssembly engine.

title: Run an existing build
content: Keep the server running; press Ctrl+C in its terminal to stop it. The launcher copies seekdb wasm database.mjs , seekdb wasm database.wasm , and engine-version.mjs into this checkout's ignored build wasm shell/ directory. It serves the shell and JavaScript API from this checkout, so reloading the page picks up source edits. The server binds to 127.0.0.1 and serves an explicit list of assets. It does not expose the repository or execute SQL.

title: Use the shell
content: The database starts automatically. Once it is ready, choose Hybrid Search or Fork Table from Examples to run its SQL immediately, or enter SQL in the prompt. Hybrid Search combines full-text matching, a category filter, and vector distance. Fork Table creates a copy and shows that changes to either table do not affect the other. Each example recreates its own demo tables in playground so it can be run repeatedly.

title: Use the shell
content: Delimiters and short commands inside strings or comments do not end a statement; close the quote or comment first, or use Ctrl+C to discard the input. Set a custom delimiter on its own line with an empty input buffer. It must be nonempty and contain no whitespace or backslashes. The delimiter is removed before SQL reaches the engine. New Instance restores the default ; delimiter. Interactive statements run in order and continue after SQL errors.

title: Use the shell
content: The Worker sends a bounded preview and consumes the rest of the result so the reported row count and session state remain correct. These display limits do not add a SQL LIMIT or stop query execution. Use LIMIT for large queries. Statement splitting supports default MySQL quoting and NO BACKSLASH ESCAPES . Use backticks for quoted identifiers; the shell does not track ANSI QUOTES mode. Custom delimiters change input parsing, not the SQL features supported by the engine.

title: Use the shell
content: Connection failures still trigger a reconnect, which rolls back uncommitted changes and resets session settings. Closing the database stops the engine; whether its data survives depends on the storage mode below.

title: Storage
content: Choose Memory or OPFS from New Instance to clear terminal output, terminate the current engine's Worker, discard its data, and start an empty database in that mode. This action does not wait for native graceful shutdown. SQL input stays disabled until the new instance is ready. Selecting the current mode also creates a new instance.

title: Storage
content: | Item | Effect | | --- | --- | | Memory | The data directory lives in Wasm memory; it is gone when the database is closed or the page is reloaded | | OPFS | The data directory lives in the origin private file system (OPFS); committed data survives reloads and browser restarts until New Instance clears it | The badge next to the database name shows memory:// or opfs:// . Reloading never clears OPFS files. New Instance explicitly starts empty.

title: Build from source
content: A static host must send Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp to enable SharedArrayBuffer for Emscripten pthreads. Use HTTPS or loopback HTTP, and serve .wasm as application/wasm and .mjs as JavaScript. Opening the HTML as a file will not work.

title: Package a release
content: This preview serves the packaged snapshot and uses a free port by default. The development servers above retain no-store so source edits remain visible on reload. The output directory must be new. Every release includes index.html , shell.html , manifest.json , and releases/ / . The hash covers every input asset, including the HTML and JavaScript, so an engine or UI change produces a new directory. The root HTML points its relative assets at that directory.

title: Package a release
content: The preview negotiates the stored representations using Accept-Encoding , and supports HEAD and conditional requests with an encoding-specific ETag .

title: Package a release
content: Copy a new version directory before replacing root HTML, and retain old version directories while existing pages may still reference them. Keep published version directories unchanged. Merely uploading the compressed files to a static host does not enable compression negotiation or these headers.

title: How SQL runs
content: This accommodates slower browser scheduling, but is not a five-minute limit on the entire startup or a guarantee against failures after a long browser suspension. Worker responses batch up to 64 events and 256 KiB of field bytes, with a 4 ms flush deadline after the first available event. An indivisible event can exceed the byte limit, subject to the existing protocol packet limits.

title: How SQL runs
content: This keeps one compiled WebAssembly.Module in the page, keyed by both URLs, for later instances. New Instance still creates fresh memory, Workers, and an engine after discarding the previous one and clearing its data. Reloading the page clears this in-page reference; release HTTP caching applies independently. API callers that omit wasmURL retain the generated loader's default behavior. The engine runs on Emscripten WasmFS.

title: How SQL runs
content: Committed data was recovered after a clean close and after a reload without one in headless Chrome; a durable commit contract on OPFS is not established yet. Database.clearPersistentStorage() removes that directory and leaves other OPFS entries of the origin alone. No database server, TCP connection, or SQL API service is required. Database.close() waits for native shutdown and keeps OPFS data.

title: How SQL runs
content: A successful discard is not a native graceful shutdown or an onExit(0) acknowledgement, and the browser does not provide a Worker termination completion event. The cleanup Worker's 15-second limit applies to retries for locked files, not to browser suspension or the total duration of storage operations. The Wasm build splits positive and INFINITY Emscripten futex waits into waits of at most one second, calling an empty JavaScript import after each timeout.
